name: Prince Jammy
hook: Trained as King Tubby's engineer, then a decade later ended dub's analogue era himself with a rhythm built from a $50 keyboard's demo button.
blurb: Lloyd James, known as Prince Jammy, had been repairing electronics and building amplifiers from his mother's house in Kingston's Waterhouse district when he joined King Tubby's studio in 1976, alongside Scientist. By 1977 he was mixing most of the rhythms that passed through Tubby's desk. In 1979 he released his own dub album, 'Kamikazi Dub', with musicians including Sly and Robbie and Augustus Pablo. In 1985, now recording as King Jammy, he produced Wayne Smith's 'Under Mi Sleng Teng', built entirely on a rock rhythm preset of a Casio MT-40 home keyboard. It was one of the first fully computerised reggae records and set off a wave of digital dancehall: it did to analogue dub what digital synthesizers and sampling were doing to popular music in general in that decade, but with a $50 preset rather than a proper studio instrument. The rhythm has since been re-recorded by more artists than any other in reggae history.
